name: octomap
desc: Efficient probabilistic 3D mapping framework based on octrees
why: Probabilistic 3D occupancy mapping with octrees is a genuinely neat data structure you can run and visualise.

brief.what_it_is: OctoMap is a C++ library for building 3D occupancy maps of an environment, stored in an octree. It takes in sensor readings from robots, such as laser scans, and folds them into a probabilistic model in which each region is marked occupied, free, or unknown. The map grows as needed and can be saved in a compact form for later use or exchange between robots. The repository also includes octovis, a visualisation library and set of tools. The metadata lists eight executables (binvox2bt, bt2vrml, compare_octrees, convert_octree, edit_octree, eval_octree_accuracy, graph2tree, log2graph), but the README I read does not describe any of them.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the library is for robotics and aims at a full 3D model with no prior assumptions about the environment. It needs to represent unknown space as well as free and occupied space, because unknown areas matter for autonomous exploration. It is developed at University of Freiburg and cited as Hornung et al., Autonomous Robots, 2013.
brief.how_it_works: The map is an octree, and each node holds a probability of occupancy that is updated from new sensor readings, which handles noise and dynamic objects. Nodes can be at different resolutions, so a coarse map can serve a high-level planner while a fine map serves a local planner. Unexplored regions are simply absent from the tree, which is how unknown space is encoded.

brief.install_notes: The homepage recommends Linux, with Mac OS and Windows also supported as a self-contained source distribution. The standard route is CMake: running it from the top level builds both octomap and octovis, and running it inside octomap/ builds only the library. Build output goes to bin and lib in the top-level directory. An alternative is vcpkg (vcpkg integrate install, then vcpkg install octomap). ROS users can use pre-compiled packages (ros.org wiki pages for octomap and octovis). Windows specifics are in octomap/README.md and octovis/README.md, which I did not fetch. The README I read lists no runtime dependencies, and I saw no first-run configuration step.
brief.standout: Unknown space is a first-class part of the model rather than an afterthought: the map records what is free, occupied, and not yet observed, and the tree grows as needed. It is also multi-resolution, so one map can serve both coarse planning and close-up visualisation.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage says OctoMap is currently maintained by Armin Hornung, and the README points to releases, a changelog, and an issue tracker. I saw no release date or last-commit date in what I fetched. The README's Travis badge points at travis-ci.org, which suggests the CI setup predates the current service.
brief.caveats: Licensing is split: octomap is New BSD, but octovis and related libraries are GPL. The README I read does not explain the eight listed executables, so their usage is unverified. Windows build details are in sub-READMEs I did not read. Its Travis CI badge may be stale. I did not check the mailing list or issue tracker for recent activity.

judge.reason: OctoMap makes unknown space explicit in a probabilistic, multi-resolution 3D map—an intriguing octree-based model with practical robotics and visualization tools.

entry.title: OctoMap
entry.tldr: A C++ library that turns robot sensor readings into a 3D map of occupied, free and unknown space, stored as an octree.
entry.deeper_look:
OctoMap builds 3D occupancy maps from sensor data such as laser scans. Space is divided into an octree, and each node holds a probability that the region is occupied. New readings update those probabilities, which is how the map copes with noise and with things that move.

The design choice that makes it interesting is that unknown space is part of the model. Regions nobody has observed are simply absent from the tree, so the map records what is free, what is occupied, and what has not been looked at yet. For a robot exploring on its own, that third category matters most, because it says where to go next. The tree grows as needed and can be saved in a compact form.

It is also multi-resolution. A coarse view of the same map can serve a high-level planner while a fine view serves a local one. The project comes out of the University of Freiburg and is cited as Hornung et al., Autonomous Robots, 2013. Its own description: "The OctoMap library implements a 3D occupancy grid mapping approach, providing data structures and mapping algorithms in C++ particularly suited for robotics."

The repository has two parts: octomap, the library, and octovis, a visualisation library and tools. Homebrew installs eight command-line executables, including converters and comparison tools for octree files. The README I read does not describe them, so start with their help output.

entry.whats_unique: Unknown space is a first-class part of the map, not an afterthought, and one map serves both coarse planning and fine detail through multi-resolution octrees.
entry.caveats: Octomap is BSD-licensed but octovis is GPL, the eight executables are undocumented in the README I read, and recent maintenance activity is unconfirmed.
